title: Checkout slowed tenfold after lunch: find out why with KQL

lines.text: 12:55 alert: POST /checkout p95 above 2,000 ms for 10 minutes (normal: about 300 ms)
12:38 release: shop-web 7.3.0 (changes: checkout shows 'you may also like' recommendations)
12:56 team lead: 'Lunchtime promo email goes out at 13:30. Scale checkout out if that is what it takes.'
monitor: POST /checkout p95 back to about 300 ms

brief.situation: You are the developer on call for shop-web at Fernhill Books (fictional). Its telemetry goes to Application Insights in the Log Analytics workspace law-shop. At 12:55 an alert says checkout's 95th-percentile time is over 2 seconds; it is usually about 300 ms. shop-web 7.3.0 went out at 12:38. A promo email at 13:30 will double checkout traffic. Find where the time goes with KQL, fix it, and show that it is fixed.
handover: shop-web has a kill switch for each new feature that it re-reads every 30 seconds; flipping one needs no deployment. Rolling back a release takes about 10 minutes.
Scaling shop-web out is one command and costs money for every extra replica.
howItWorks: Run queries and commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's queries run; each is a fixed query with its own result.
Each query or change takes your time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The incident keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows the app and its dependencies with a status in words. Results appear in the terminal.
When you declare it fixed, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command or change takes, and when the fictional incident develops, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The promo email goes out at 13:30, 34 minutes after the alert.

writeup.question: For the incident record: how the queries led you to the cause, what you changed and why not scaling, and how you showed it was fixed.

parts.label: From symptom to cause
parts.criteria: Uses a percentile trend (not an average) to date the change, a dependency breakdown by Target to find recs-api slow while SQL and the cache are normal, and the version or a single operation's trace to tie it to 7.3.0's new synchronous call.
parts.modelAnswer: percentiles by 10-minute bin showed p95 jump from about 300 to 4,000 ms at 12:40. AppDependencies by Target showed recs-api at 3.9 s p95 with failures while sql-orders and redis-cart were normal, and only 7.3.0 calls recs-api from POST /checkout; one operation's trace put 4.17 of 4.2 s in that call.

parts.label: The fix
parts.criteria: Turns off the new recommendations call (kill switch) or rolls back; explains that adding web replicas or restarting recs-api does not help when every request waits on a slow dependency.
parts.modelAnswer: I switched checkout recommendations off, which takes effect in 30 seconds without a deploy. More shop-web replicas would each still wait 4 seconds for recs-api.

parts.label: Proof and prevention
parts.criteria: Re-runs the p95 query after the fix, and proposes a timeout or asynchronous load for the dependency and an alert on dependency latency.
parts.modelAnswer: p95 for POST /checkout over the last 5 minutes is back to about 300 ms. Next: call recs-api with a short timeout and render checkout without it, and alert on its p95.

fixed.body: Percentiles dated the change, the dependency breakdown named recs-api, the version tied it to 7.3.0, and a kill switch fixed it without a deploy.

scoring.modelReasoning: A p95 trend by 10-minute bin dates the jump to 12:40, just after 7.3.0. Summarizing AppDependencies by Target shows recs-api at 3.9 s p95 with failures while SQL and Redis are normal; by AppVersion, only 7.3.0 calls it from checkout, and one operation's trace puts 4.17 of 4.2 s in that call. Turn the new call off with its kill switch (or roll back), then prove it with the p95 query. More web replicas would each wait on the same slow call.
